exercises.prompt: Wei and Lucía want to know whose pencil is longer. What is the **fair** way to compare them?

options.label: Put them side by side, with their ends lined up at the same starting line
options.feedback: Yes! With the ends lined up, the pencil that sticks out further is longer.

options.label: Put them side by side anywhere and see which end is further to the right
options.feedback: If one pencil starts further along, it can look longer even when it is shorter. Line up the starting ends first.

options.label: The brighter pencil is longer
options.feedback: Colour has nothing to do with length! Put them side by side and compare.

hints: Think of a running race: why does everyone start at the same line?
What happens if one pencil starts further along than the other?
exercises.solution: Put the pencils **side by side with their ends lined up** at the same starting line. Then the one that sticks out further at the other end is the longer one. If they don't start together, the comparison can trick you.

exercises.prompt: A leaf lies along a ruler. Its stem is at **0** and its tip is at **7**. How many centimetres long is the leaf?

feedback.message: It looks like you counted the marks 0, 1, 2, …, 7. Count the spaces between the marks instead.
Count again from 0: the first centimetre is the space from 0 to 1.

hints: When something starts at 0, the number at its other end tells you its length.
Read the number at the tip of the leaf.
exercises.solution: The leaf starts at **0**, so the number at its tip is its length: **7** centimetres. (There are 8 marks from 0 to 7, but only 7 spaces, and the spaces are the centimetres.)

exercises.prompt: A crayon does **not** start at 0. One end is at **3** and the other end is at **12**. How many centimetres long is the crayon?

feedback.message: 12 is where the crayon *ends*. But it started at 3, not at 0. What do you need to take away?
Did you count the marks 3, 4, …, 12? There is one more mark than spaces. Count the spaces.
Adding 3 and 12 makes it longer than the ruler shows. The part from 0 to 3 is *not* under the crayon.

hints: The number 12 counts the centimetres from 0 to 12. Are all of them under the crayon?
The 3 centimetres from 0 to 3 are not under the crayon. Take them away.
exercises.solution: The number 12 counts 12 centimetres from 0. The first 3 of them, from 0 to 3, are not under the crayon. So the crayon is $12 - 3 = 9$ centimetres long. You can also count on from 3: 4, 5, 6, …, 12 is **9** steps.

exercises.prompt: Amara measures the same table twice: once with **paper clips** and once with her **hand spans**. Which measurement gives the **bigger number**?

options.label: Paper clips
options.feedback: Yes! Paper clips are smaller than hand spans, so it takes more of them to cover the table.

options.label: Hand spans
options.feedback: A hand span is bigger than a paper clip. Do you need more big units or more small units to cover the same table?

options.label: Both give the same number
options.feedback: The table stays the same, but the units are different sizes. Different-sized units give different numbers.

hints: Which is smaller: a paper clip or a hand span?
If each unit is small, do you need many of them or only a few?
exercises.solution: **Paper clips.** A paper clip is much smaller than a hand span, so many more clips than hand spans fit along the table. The smaller the unit, the bigger the number. (In the lesson: 24 clips but only 6 hand spans.)

exercises.prompt: A pencil is really 5 paper clips long. Jomo lays clips along it, but leaves **gaps** between them. What happens to his count?

options.label: He counts too few clips
options.feedback: Yes! With gaps, the clips reach the end of the pencil too soon, so he counts fewer than 5.

options.label: He counts too many clips
options.feedback: That happens when the clips overlap. With gaps, do the clips reach the end sooner or later?

options.label: He still gets exactly 5
options.feedback: The gaps cover part of the pencil without being counted. Will he still need 5 clips to reach the end?

hints: Each gap covers a bit of pencil that no clip is counting.
So do the clips reach the end of the pencil sooner or later than they should?
exercises.solution: The gaps cover part of the pencil but are not counted, so the clips reach the end too soon. Jomo counts **too few** clips — maybe only 4. Overlapping clips do the opposite and give too many.

exercises.prompt: Gideon's game: is this statement true or false? *"When I bend a string into a wiggly shape, it becomes shorter."*

options.label: True
options.feedback: The ends are closer together, but was any string cut off? Straighten it again and check.

options.label: False
options.feedback: Yes! Bending moves the ends closer together, but the string is just as long. Nothing was cut off.

hints: Was any piece of the string cut off when you bent it?
If you straighten the string again, how long is it?
exercises.solution: **False.** Bending changes where the ends of the string are, but not how long the string is. Straighten it and it reaches exactly as far as before. In the Lean file this is the theorem `bend_keeps_length`.

exercises.prompt: The rope is longer than the stick. The stick is longer than the pencil. Which statement **must** be true?

options.label: The rope is longer than the pencil
options.feedback: Yes! The rope is longer than the stick, which is longer than the pencil. You did not even need to put the rope next to the pencil.

options.label: The pencil is longer than the rope
options.feedback: Draw the three in a row from longest to shortest. Where do the rope and the pencil go?

options.label: We can't tell until we put the rope next to the pencil
options.feedback: We can tell! The stick sits in between: shorter than the rope, longer than the pencil.

hints: Put the three in order from longest to shortest.
The stick is in the middle. What does that tell you about the rope and the pencil?
exercises.solution: In order from longest to shortest: rope, stick, pencil. So **the rope is longer than the pencil**. This rule — if A is longer than B and B is longer than C, then A is longer than C — always works.

exercises.prompt: On a clock, the **long hand points to 6**, and the **short hand is halfway between 9 and 10**. What time is it?

options.label: Half past 9 (9:30)
options.feedback: Yes! The long hand at 6 means half past, and the short hand has gone halfway from 9 towards 10.

options.label: Half past 10 (10:30)
options.feedback: The short hand has not reached 10 yet — it is only halfway there. Which hour has it passed?

options.label: 9 o'clock (9:00)
options.feedback: At 9 o'clock the long hand points to 12, not to 6.

options.label: Half past 6 (6:30)
options.feedback: The long hand shows the minutes, not the hour. The short hand shows the hour.

hints: The long hand shows the minutes. Where does it point at half past?
The short hand shows the hour. Which hour has it just passed?
exercises.solution: The long hand pointing to 6 means it has gone halfway round: **half past**. The short hand has passed 9 and is halfway to 10. So it is **half past 9**, written 9:30.

exercises.prompt: It is 2 o'clock. Counting on in half hours like Margaret (2:30, 3:00, …), how many **half hours** is it until 4 o'clock?

feedback.message: 2 is the number of whole *hours* from 2 o'clock to 4 o'clock. How many *half* hours fit in each hour?
Count the jumps, not the times: 2:00 → 2:30 → 3:00 → 3:30 → 4:00.

hints: Two half hours make one hour.
Count the jumps: 2:00 → 2:30 is one jump. Keep going until 4:00.
exercises.solution: Counting on: 2:00 → 2:30 → 3:00 → 3:30 → 4:00. That is **4** jumps of half an hour. It makes sense: 2 hours, and 2 half hours in each hour, gives 4 half hours.
